Passage 1: The Data Dilemma: Understanding Numbers in Education

In the small town of Riverton, a local school recently introduced a new data system to track student progress. The system collects weekly quiz scores, attendance records, and homework completion rates. Teachers and administrators hoped that this data would help them identify students who need extra support. However, as the first semester progressed, it became clear that interpreting the data was more complex than expected. The school had invested considerable time and money in the system, and staff members were eager to see results, but they soon discovered that raw numbers alone could not tell the full story. Understanding the data required patience, training, and a willingness to look beneath the surface.

A
One major issue was the comparison of scores across different classes. For example, Class A had an average quiz score of 85%, while Class B had an average of 78%. At first glance, Class A seemed to be performing better. But when teachers looked closer, they noticed that Class A's quizzes were shorter and covered fewer topics. Class B's quizzes were longer and more challenging. Therefore, comparing the averages directly was misleading. The teachers realized that they needed to consider the difficulty of the assessments before drawing conclusions. They began to review the content and length of each quiz, and they agreed that future comparisons would require a common standard. This experience taught them that a single number can hide important differences in what is actually being measured.

B
Another challenge involved the number of students represented by the data. In Class C, only 15 students took the quiz, whereas Class D had 30 students. A single very high or very low score in Class C could significantly affect the class average, while in Class D, individual scores had less impact. This statistical concept, known as the effect of sample size, was not initially understood by all staff. Some teachers assumed that a small class's average was just as reliable as a large class's average. They learned that smaller samples often produce more variable results. To address this, the school organized a short training session on basic statistics, where teachers practiced interpreting averages from groups of different sizes. They also discussed how to communicate uncertainty when reporting results to parents and students.

C
The school also tracked homework completion. Overall, 80% of students completed their homework regularly. However, when the data was broken down by grade level, a different picture emerged. In Grade 9, 90% of students completed homework, but in Grade 10, only 70% did. This drop was concerning. The teachers investigated and found that Grade 10 students had more part-time jobs and extracurricular commitments. Thus, the overall figure hid important variations between groups. The staff concluded that aggregated data can mask underlying trends. They decided that future reports would always include a breakdown by grade level and, where possible, by other relevant factors such as attendance patterns. This way, they could respond to the specific needs of each group rather than relying on a single overall number.

D
Finally, the school considered how to use the data to help students. Rather than simply ranking classes, they decided to use the data to identify specific skills that needed reinforcement. For instance, many students struggled with fractions, so the math department organized extra workshops. They also used the data to monitor the effectiveness of these workshops over time. By comparing pre-workshop and post-workshop scores, they could see whether the intervention was working. This approach focused on improvement rather than judgment. Teachers reported that students felt less pressured and more willing to ask for help when they knew the data was being used to support them rather than to label them. The school plans to expand this model to other subjects in the coming year.

E
Reflecting on the semester, the principal noted that data is a tool, not an answer. It requires careful interpretation and context. The school plans to continue using data but with more training for teachers on statistical literacy. They also intend to involve students in understanding their own data, helping them set personal learning goals. In this way, data can become a means of empowerment rather than a source of anxiety. The principal emphasized that the goal is not to collect more data but to use it more wisely. Teachers have begun to share their experiences with one another, creating a culture of collaborative inquiry that supports continuous improvement.

The Riverton case illustrates a common challenge in education: numbers can inform decisions, but only if they are understood correctly. As one teacher put it, "Data is like a flashlight; it illuminates the path, but you still need to know where you are going."

Passage 2: The Cost of Free Shipping: A Simulated Case Study in Data Interpretation

A. In 2022, the online home goods retailer GreenSprout Home faced a puzzling problem. Although its total revenue had grown by 18% compared to the previous year, its net profit had fallen by 7%. This divergence between the top line and the bottom line was unusual for a company that had been expanding steadily, and it raised concerns among senior managers. The marketing team celebrated the revenue increase, pointing to strong customer demand and successful promotional campaigns, but the finance department was worried. To understand this gap, the company decided to analyse its customer data more carefully. They focused on the effect of their free shipping policy, which had been introduced in early 2021. The policy offered free delivery on all orders over $50. At first, it seemed like a great success: the number of orders rose sharply, and customer satisfaction scores improved. However, the finance team suspected that the policy was attracting many small orders that were expensive to fulfil. They needed evidence. Rather than relying on impressions or anecdotal reports from warehouse staff, they asked the data team to carry out a structured comparison of customer behaviour before and after the policy took effect. This approach reflected a broader shift in the company towards evidence-based management, in which decisions would be justified by measurable data rather than by intuition or seniority. The data team was given access to eighteen months of transaction records, including order values, delivery costs, return histories and repeat-purchase information, and was asked to present its findings to a joint meeting of the marketing and finance departments. The request was deliberately broad, so that the analysis would not be shaped by the assumptions of either department, and the team was told to report any pattern that could explain the profit gap, even if it contradicted the marketing team's optimistic interpretation of the sales figures.

B. The data team compared two groups of customers: those who spent just over $50 (the “borderline” group) and those who spent significantly more, around $80 or above (the “high-value” group). The results were striking. The borderline group placed 35% more orders than the high-value group, but the average profit per order for the borderline group was only $2.50, whereas for the high-value group it was $12.00. This meant that each borderline order contributed very little to covering fixed costs such as warehousing, packaging and delivery. Moreover, the borderline group returned items much more frequently: their return rate was 22%, compared to 8% for the high-value group. Each return added further handling and shipping costs, which reduced the already thin margin on these orders. The data also showed that customers in the borderline group were less likely to buy again within three months. In contrast, high-value customers often became repeat buyers, building a long-term relationship with the brand. The team concluded that free shipping was encouraging a large number of low-profit, high-return orders. This was eroding overall profitability, even though the total number of orders looked impressive on paper. The comparison made the hidden cost of the policy visible: growth in order volume had been bought at the price of weaker margins and higher service costs, and the two effects had cancelled out much of the apparent gain. Presenting the two groups side by side allowed managers to see that the same policy could produce very different outcomes depending on the size of the order, and it turned a vague suspicion into a clear, measurable explanation of the falling profit.

C. Based on these findings, GreenSprout Home decided to change its policy. Instead of offering free shipping on all orders over $50, they introduced a tiered system. Orders between $50 and $75 would now incur a small delivery fee of $3.99, while orders over $75 would still enjoy free shipping. The aim was to discourage very small, costly orders without punishing loyal customers who spent more. The company also started a loyalty programme that rewarded repeat customers with points, giving high-value shoppers an additional reason to return. After six months, the results were positive. The number of borderline orders fell by 15%, but the high-value orders increased by 10%. The average profit per order rose to $8.50, and the return rate dropped to 12%. Customer satisfaction remained stable, suggesting that the small delivery fee did not damage the brand's reputation. The finance director noted, “We learned that not all revenue growth is good growth. Understanding the data behind the numbers is essential.” The case shows how comparing different customer segments and using quantitative evidence can lead to better business decisions. It also illustrates a practical lesson for other retailers: a policy that looks generous and popular on the surface may conceal costs that only careful measurement can reveal, and adjusting the threshold rather than abandoning the benefit allowed the company to protect both its margins and its customers' goodwill.

Passage 3: The Data We Trust: A Community Library's Reading Survey

A
In the small town of Riverton, the community library decided to find out how its members used the library’s reading services. The head librarian, Ms. Chen, designed a survey with ten questions. She wanted to understand which services were most popular and which groups of people were not being reached. The survey was given to 500 members over a period of four weeks. Of these, 320 members returned completed forms. Ms. Chen was pleased with this response rate, which was higher than she had expected. She believed that the results would help the library plan better for the next year. A good response rate matters because it makes the findings more reliable, and Ms. Chen hoped the data would guide decisions about staffing, opening hours and the range of materials on offer.

B
The survey asked members how often they visited the library, which sections they used most, and what improvements they would like. The results showed that 45% of respondents visited the library at least once a week. Another 30% visited two or three times a month. The remaining 25% visited less than once a month. When asked about their favourite sections, 40% chose fiction, 35% chose non-fiction, and 25% chose children’s books. Ms. Chen noted that the children’s section was used by more people than she had thought. She said, “This is more than we expected, and it shows that families are a key group for us.” This finding encouraged her to consider adding more seating and activities for younger readers and their parents.

C
However, the survey also revealed some gaps. Only 15% of respondents said they used the library’s online resources. When asked why, many said they did not know these resources existed. In addition, members aged 65 and over were less likely to visit the library than younger members. Only 10% of respondents were in this age group, although they make up 20% of the town’s population. Ms. Chen concluded that the library needed to improve its communication with older residents and to promote its online services more actively. She planned to hold a series of workshops to introduce the online catalogue to members. She also suggested that leaflets and notices in local shops could help spread the word to people who rarely came into the building.

D
One interesting finding was about reading habits. The survey asked members how many books they read in a month. The average was two books per month. However, there was a difference between age groups: members under 30 read an average of three books per month, while those over 60 read an average of one book per month. Ms. Chen was not surprised by this, as she had read similar findings in other surveys. She emphasised that the library should offer large-print books and audiobooks for older readers, as these formats might be more accessible to them. She added that staff could also help older members find titles that suited their interests, since personal recommendations often encouraged people to read more.

E
Ms. Chen also compared the results with a similar survey conducted five years ago. In that survey, only 20% of members used the library at least once a week. Now, the figure is 45%. This suggests that the library’s recent efforts to attract more visitors have been successful. However, the number of members using online resources has not increased much; five years ago it was 12%, and now it is 15%. Ms. Chen believes that the library must do more to keep up with the digital age. She has proposed a new budget for technology improvements, which the library board will discuss next month. The proposal includes faster computers, a clearer website and training for staff so that they can answer members’ questions about digital services.

F
In her report, Ms. Chen wrote: “The survey shows that our members value the library, but we must not be complacent. We need to reach out to older residents and to those who are not yet using our online services. The data help us to see where we are doing well and where we need to improve.” She also noted that the survey would be repeated every two years to track changes over time. The library board praised her work and agreed to fund the workshops and the technology improvements. The community library in Riverton is now seen as a model for other small libraries in the region. Other librarians have asked Ms. Chen for copies of her questionnaire and her report, and she is happy to share them so that similar towns can learn from Riverton’s experience.
